title: Growing lovage
subtitle: A tall perennial herb with a strong celery-like flavour used in soups and stocks.
excerpt: Lovage is a large perennial herb that produces celery-flavoured leaves from April to October. One well-grown plant produces more than most households need. Cut back hard in midsummer to get a second flush of fresh, tender leaves.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Jekka McVicar, The Complete Herb Book (1994). Cutting-back technique from Roger Phillips and Nicky Foy, Herbs (1990). UK hardiness data widely documented in horticultural reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: Propagating a clump-forming perennial by splitting the root crown into sections, each with roots and growing buds attached. Carried out in autumn or early spring when the plant is dormant. Lovage, comfrey, and sorrel can all be propagated this way.

content.text: Lovage is a vigorous perennial herb that grows to 1.5 to 2 m tall in a good season. It tastes strongly of celery and is used in soups, stocks, and stews. One plant is enough for most families. The leaves, stems, seeds, and roots are all edible.

Lovage grows best in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun or partial shade. It tolerates more shade than most herbs. In dry soils it dies back early in summer. Mulch heavily each spring to retain moisture. Hardy to H7 and fully frost-tolerant.

Buy a pot-grown plant in spring or sow fresh seed in autumn (lovage seed needs a cold period to germinate reliably). Plant out in March to April. In its first year it grows to about 60 cm; from the second year it reaches full height. Propagate by

Harvest individual stems from April onwards, cutting at the base. The leaves are strongest in flavour before the plant flowers. In midsummer (late June to July), cut the whole plant to 15 cm above the ground. This removes the coarse flowering stems and prompts a second flush of fresh, tender leaves that lasts through autumn.

The cut-back also prevents the plant self-seeding, which it does freely and can become a weed problem. If you want seed for cooking or propagation, leave one stem to set seed then cut it and collect before it drops.

attrs.title: Lovage in cooking
attrs.body: Use lovage sparingly: it is much stronger in flavour than fresh celery. A single stem is enough to flavour a pot of soup. The leaves can replace celery in any cooked dish. Young stems are sometimes blanched and eaten like celery, though they are stronger in flavour. The dried leaves keep well and can be used in winter when the plant is dormant.
